summary: This informational memo describes the Data Link Switching Client Access Protocol, used between workstations and routers to carry SNA and NetBIOS traffic over TCP sessions. It replaced RFC 2106.

eli5.summary: Old office programs speak their own language, so this protocol wraps their messages in Internet envelopes for the trip.

questions: data link switching client access protocol
how does dcap assign a mac address
subtitle: How workstations talk to a DLSw router as clients, so SNA and NetBIOS traffic can ride over TCP without one peer session per PC.

tldr.problem: Running full DLSw on every workstation means one TCP session to the central router per workstation, which does not scale, and DLSw is a switch-to-switch protocol that is inefficient on a workstation.
tldr.mechanism: DCAP turns the workstations into clients of a router acting as a server. A client opens a single TCP connection to the server and exchanges small framed messages with a 4-byte header, while the server keeps one peer connection to the central site.
tldr.outcome: The central router sees far fewer peers, and the server can hand out MAC addresses to clients that have none. The memo is Informational and replaces RFC 2106.

today: RFC 2114 is an Informational memo, not an Internet standard, and it obsoletes RFC 2106. The metadata lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why DCAP Exists
sections.content:
After the Data Link Switching protocol (DLSw, RFC 1795) was published, some software vendors started to implement it on workstations. That raised two concerns. The first is scalability: the number of TCP sessions to the DLSw router grows in direct proportion to the number of workstations. The second is efficiency: DLSw is a switch-to-switch protocol, so it is not efficient when run on a workstation.

The Data Link Switching Client Access Protocol (DCAP) answers both. It introduces a hierarchy: the workstations become clients of the router, which acts as a server, instead of being peers of it. The protocol between client and server is also lighter than full DLSw. The memo says it is used between workstations and routers to carry SNA and NetBIOS traffic over TCP sessions.
sections.eli5: Having every computer call the main router on its own line gets crowded. DCAP gives them one shared helper to talk to, and the helper uses simple messages.

sections.title: The Client/Server Model
sections.content:
In a plain DLSw setup each workstation is a DLSw peer of the central site router. With DCAP, workstations are DCAP clients attached to a DCAP server, which is a DLSw router. The server keeps a single peer connection to the central site router, so the central router sees one peer instead of one per workstation.

Most DCAP frames are modelled on existing DLSw frames and carry similar names and the same functions, so the DLSw state machine is used to handle them. Some DLSw frames that DCAP does not need are dropped. Two frames are new and give negative acknowledgment: I_CANNOT_REACH and START_DL_FAILED.
sections.eli5: Many small computers talk to one local helper, and only the helper talks to the big central machine. Fewer callers means less chaos.

sections.title: Dynamic Address Resolution
sections.content:
A DLSw workstation needs a MAC address to reach a front end processor on a LAN. A workstation dialled in over PPP may only have an IP address, so an administrator would have to define a unique virtual MAC address for each one. DCAP avoids that with Dynamic Address Resolution: the server can assign a MAC address to a client dynamically.

When a client starts a session, it sends a direct request to the server containing the destination MAC address and destination SAP. The client can state its own MAC address or ask the server to assign one. The server's IP address must be pre-configured on the workstation. If several servers are configured, the request can go to all of them and the first to respond is used.

When a server starts a session toward a client, the client's MAC address must already be registered at the server, either by configuration or by registration. Both the MAC and IP addresses are registered.
sections.eli5: If a computer has no name tag, the helper hands it one. If the helper wants to call a computer first, it needs to have written that computer's name down beforehand.

sections.title: TCP Connection and Optional Multicast
sections.content:
Client and server communicate over TCP, and a TCP session must exist before any frame is sent. The default parameters are socket family AF_INET, socket type SOCK_STREAM and port 1973. There is only one TCP connection between a client and a server, used for both reading and writing. If both sides try to open a connection at the same time, the session of the initiator with the lower IP address is kept and the other is closed.

Multicast and unicast over UDP are optional. Two multicast addresses are reserved: the server listens on 224.0.1.49 and the client listens on 224.0.1.50. CAN_U_REACH may be sent by multicast only, I_CAN_REACH by unicast only, and DATA_FRAME by either. All other frames travel only over TCP.

With multicast, a client does not need the server's address configured. It multicasts CAN_U_REACH, a server that can reach the destination answers by unicast with I_CAN_REACH, and the client then opens a TCP connection to the first server that answered. In the other direction, a server looking for an unknown client multicasts CAN_U_REACH and the client with the matching MAC address replies by unicast. NetBIOS name queries (NAME_QUERY, ADD_NAME_QUERY) can be carried in DATA_FRAME and multicast in the same way.
sections.eli5: Normally a computer knows its helper's phone number. With the optional shout-out feature, it can yell into the room and the first helper who can help calls back.

sections.title: Frame Format and Message Types
sections.content:
Each DCAP frame has up to three parts: a DCAP header, optional DCAP data that depends on the message type, and optional user data. The header is 4 bytes. Its first byte holds the Protocol ID (the first 4 bits, set to 1000) and the Version Number (the next 4 bits, set to 0001). The second byte is the message type, and the last two bytes are the total packet length, which counts the header, DCAP data and user data. The minimum length is 4.

The memo lists 21 message types, from CAN_U_REACH (0x01) to PEER_TEST_RSP (0x1E). The DCAP data for each family of frames carries things such as a target MAC address and SAP, session IDs, a largest frame size, an initial window size, or a reason code. Senders must set reserved fields to zero and receivers ignore them.

The START_DL family also carries origin and target session IDs, because DCAP does not use a three-way handshake to establish a link station. The window size and flow-control flags are used the same way as in DLSw.
sections.eli5: Every message starts with a tiny label saying what kind of message it is and how long it is. Then comes any extra detail, then the real content.

sections.title: Session Lifecycle and Keepalive
sections.content:
Right after the TCP session comes up, client and server exchange CAP_XCHANGE frames and must finish before other frames are sent. The frame carries the client's MAC address, or zero if it has none, in which case the server assigns one. Either side can send command frames, and the exchange stops when one side sends a response with the agreed MAC address. A flag byte announces capabilities such as NetBIOS support (0x01), TCP listen mode (0x02) and command versus response (0x04). Optional control vectors include SAP_LIST (up to 16 SAPs) and VENDOR_CODE, and unknown vectors should be ignored.

A normal session then runs: the client sends CAN_U_REACH, the server explores the LAN and answers I_CAN_REACH, and START_DL / DL_STARTED create the circuit. The server's recommended explorer retry values are 5 seconds and 5 times, after which it returns I_CANNOT_REACH (or START_DL_FAILED for circuit setup). XID_FRAME, CONTACT_STN and STN_CONTACTED follow, then INFO_FRAME carries data. HALT_DL and DL_HALTED end the circuit and the TCP session stays up.

To close the peer, CLOSE_PEER_REQ carries a reason code: system shutdown (0x01), suspend (0x02) or no MAC address available (0x03). Peer-level keepalive uses PEER_TEST_REQ (optional to send) and PEER_TEST_RSP (must be implemented). The recommended wait is 60 seconds and 3 tries before the TCP session and its circuits are closed.
sections.eli5: First the two sides introduce themselves, then they open a chat line, talk, hang up the chat, and finally say goodbye. A regular "are you still there?" check makes sure nobody left.
